text: Revisionism is the practice of taking a second look at how a period or event is usually remembered and arguing that the standard story is wrong or incomplete. A revisionist historian might claim a famous villain had a point, or that a celebrated victory mattered less than people think The Economist says a revisionist look at the 2010s shows they quietly shaped business today.

An artefact (American spelling: artifact) is an object made by people that survives from an earlier time, like a pot dug up by archaeologists or a letter in a museum. It can also describe an idea or document that feels like a relic of its era. The 2019 Business Roundtable pledge now reads like a relic of a more idealistic time.

Something exacting demands great care, precision or effort. An exacting coach accepts nothing sloppy, and an exacting test leaves no room for guesses. Effective altruism tries to measure very precisely how much good each action does.
An embarrassment is something that makes people feel ashamed or awkward. Calling the 2010s an embarrassment means the decade is remembered with a wince, even though it was important.
Exuberance is overflowing, excited energy and confidence. Executive exuberance means bosses were feeling boldly optimistic and spending freely before the 2010s brought discipline.
Cringeworthy describes something so awkward or embarrassing that it makes you wince. The Economist admits the 2010s were cringeworthy but still revolutionary.
A drunk tank is a jail cell where people are held until they sober up. Saying bankers spent the decade in it is a joke about how banks were punished and humbled after the financial crisis.
Corner offices are the big, prestigious offices where top executives sit. The phrase stands for the bosses of a company.
This is a joke on annus horribilis, Latin for a horrible year. Decennium means a ten-year period, so the phrase means a horrible decade.
Activist investors buy a large stake in a company and then push its leaders to change course, for example by cutting costs or selling parts of the business.
A company's board is the group of directors, elected by the shareholders, who oversee the top managers and can hire or fire the chief executive.
Shale is a rock that holds oil and gas. New drilling methods, fracking and horizontal wells, let America extract huge amounts from it in the 2010s.
A net exporter sells more of something abroad than it buys from abroad. America becoming a net exporter of energy meant it produced more than it used.
A special-purpose vehicle is a separate company created for one job, such as owning a single project, so that its debts and risks stay apart from its parent company.
Offshore here means based in another country, often one with lighter taxes or rules, such as the Cayman Islands or Bermuda.
Gig workers do short, flexible jobs paid task by task, like driving for Uber or delivering for DoorDash, instead of holding a regular full-time job.
The Stasi was East Germany's feared secret police. A lanyard is the cord that holds an office badge. The joke is about workplace officials who enforce company culture.

t: bring their whole selves to work
forms: bring their whole selves to work
text: This was a popular workplace slogan of the 2010s, urging employees to be fully themselves at work instead of hiding their personal side.
A panopticon is a building designed so that a single guard can see every prisoner. Here it jokes that the modern open-plan office makes everyone watchable.
Soft-furnished means decorated with sofas, cushions and comfy chairs, as in trendy offices that try to feel like living rooms.
A dashboard is a screen that gathers a company's key numbers and charts in one place, like a car dashboard for a business.
Hot desks are desks that nobody owns. Workers sit at whichever one is free that day instead of having their own.
The writer compares the constant ping of Slack messages to distant gunfire: an endless, nagging rattle of interruptions.
Ripest means most ready, like fruit about to be picked. Silicon Valley is the most ready subject for a fresh look at the 2010s.
Effective altruism is a movement that uses evidence and math to decide how to do the most good with your time and money, and it grew out of Oxford and Silicon Valley.
A calculus is a system of calculation. An ethical calculus tries to work out right and wrong by adding up the good and harm of each choice.
Cloisters are covered walkways around a monastery courtyard. Here the word stands for the quiet, sheltered world of elite universities.
Universal basic income is the idea that the government pays every citizen a regular sum of money, with no conditions, so that everyone has a floor to stand on.
Antitrust laws stop companies from becoming so big or powerful that they crush competition and hurt customers.
This phrase describes the belief that large companies are harmful just because they are large, even if their prices are low.
A wealth tax charges a small percentage each year on everything a rich person owns, not just on what they earn.
Thomas Piketty is a French economist whose book Capital in the Twenty-First Century argued that wealth gets more concentrated over time.
Delaware is a small US state where most big American companies are legally registered, because its business laws and courts are well tested.
The Business Roundtable is a lobbying group of the chief executives of big American companies. In 2019 it said firms should serve all stakeholders, not just shareholders.
Stakeholders are everyone affected by a company: workers, customers, neighbors and the community, not just the people who own its shares.
Shareholders are the people who own shares, which are small slices of ownership, in a company.
High-mindedness means having noble principles and aiming at ideals. The writer hints it can sound a little pious.
Karl Marx wrote that people make history, but not under conditions they choose. The writer twists the line to say businesspeople inherit ideas from the 2010s.
Private-equity funds raise money from investors, buy companies, try to improve them and sell them later, ideally for a profit.
ESG stands for environmental, social and governance: a way of judging companies on pollution, treatment of people and how well they are run.
McKinsey is one of the world's best-known consulting firms, hired by companies and governments for advice.
A B-Corp is a company that has paid to be certified as meeting high standards of social and environmental responsibility.

t: Japanese soldiers who ignored the end of the second world war
forms: Japanese soldiers who ignored the end of the second world war
text: A few Japanese soldiers kept fighting in remote jungles for decades after 1945 because they refused to believe the war was over. The writer says some ESG fans are like that.
Normal eyesight is called 20/20 vision. 20/10 is sharper than normal, and the writer plays on it with a nod to the 2010s and seeing them clearly.
Sam Bankman-Fried founded the crypto exchange FTX, which collapsed in 2022, and he was later convicted of fraud.
Elizabeth Holmes founded the blood-testing start-up Theranos and was convicted of fraud after its technology turned out not to work.
The euro zone is the group of European countries that use the euro as their money.
Early Twitter limited posts to 140 characters. The line jokes that critics said the 2010s gave us nothing but tiny messages.
